newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPALS -- DOWN AT LEAST ONE POINT.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPALS -- DOWN AT LEAST ONE POINT.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond prices dropped at least a point Friday after a worrisome report on inflation, but traders said activity was muted.

"If you tried to sell anything you'd probably be down at least a point, but nobody's willing to sell," one trader said. "Everytime the market's gone down it's paid to hang on because it went back up."

Friday's freefall began after the National Association of Purchasing Management's July manufacturing report sent an inflation scare through the market at mid-morning. It jolted investors already unnerved by a strong employment report earlier in the day.
The NAPM survey's headline index showed a sharp rise, moving to 58.6 in July from 55.7 in June. The price component also jumped significantly, another indication of rising price pressure.

The Treasury market, which sold off modestly after a stronger-than-expected July employment report, went into a sharp decline falling NAPM. The government long bond was off nearly two points at 102-15/32, driving the yield up to 6.44 percent.

Futures markets also sold off sharply at mid-morning. The September municipal contract lost 1-17/32 to 120-20/32, while September T-bonds dropped 1-18/32 to 115-6/32. The MOB spread widened to 174 ticks from 173 at the close on Thursday.
Actively traded secondary market issues included Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority 5.0s of 2024, which were bid at 5.41 percent, up nine basis points.
In follow-through action from Thursday, PaineWebber Inc said it had a $32 million balance on Wisconsin's $101 million general obligation bond deal.
And Lehman Brothers said Colorado's $822 million E-470 Public Highway Authority revenue bond deal, the largest new issue of the week, was free to trade.
